title: Food Shopping and Grocery Stores
objectives: Navigate an American grocery store confidently, including understanding store layout and sections
Read food labels to understand serving size, calories, ingredients, and expiry dates
Compare prices and use unit pricing to find value for money
Use quantifiers (some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little) correctly when shopping

reading_passage.title: Your First Trip to an American Grocery Store
reading_passage.text:
Walking into an American supermarket for the first time can be an overwhelming experience. Stores like Fred Meyer, Safeway, Winco, and Trader Joe's are typically much larger than shops in Somalia or other East African countries, with dozens of aisles dedicated to specific product categories. Most stores organise their layout with fresh produce near the entrance, followed by dairy, meat, frozen foods, and dry goods in the interior aisles.

Reading food labels is an essential skill. In the United States, all packaged foods are required to display a Nutrition Facts label, which shows the serving size, the number of calories, and the amounts of fat, protein, carbohydrates, sodium, and vitamins per serving. The ingredients are also listed in order from most to least — if sugar appears near the top, the product contains a large amount of it.

For newcomers on a limited budget, comparing unit prices is very useful. Unit prices — shown on the shelf label — display the cost per ounce, pound, or litre, making it easy to compare products of different sizes. The store brand is usually significantly cheaper than name brands and is often made by the same manufacturer.

Discount grocery stores like WinCo Foods offer much lower prices than standard supermarkets, but they typically require you to bag your own groceries and do not accept credit cards. Some newcomers also access the Oregon Food Bank, which operates distribution sites throughout Portland and provides free food to anyone in need — no proof of income is required.
reading_passage.source: Adapted from newcomer consumer literacy materials produced by Lutheran Community Services Northwest and Oregon Department of Human Services, Portland, 2023

glossary.meaning: a passage between rows of shelves in a supermarket or shop
fresh fruit and vegetables sold in a supermarket
the required information panel on packaged food in the US showing calorie and nutrient content
the cost of a product per standard unit of measurement (per ounce, pound, or litre), shown on the shelf label
a product made for and sold under the supermarket's own name, usually cheaper than name-brand equivalents

comprehension.question: According to the passage, how are ingredients listed on American food labels?
comprehension.answer: In order from most to least — the ingredient present in the largest amount appears first on the list.

comprehension.question: What does the author imply when they say store brands are 'often made by the same manufacturer' as name brands?
comprehension.answer: The author implies that paying more for a name brand does not necessarily mean better quality — the cheaper store brand product may be identical in content, so choosing the store brand is a smart way to save money.

comprehension.question: What is a 'unit price,' according to the passage?
comprehension.answer: The cost of a product per standard unit of measurement — such as per ounce, pound, or litre — shown on the shelf label so shoppers can compare the true value of products in different sizes.

comprehension.question: Why does the author mention the Oregon Food Bank at the end of the passage?
comprehension.answer: To make sure newcomers know that a free food resource exists — removing the assumption that they must spend money on groceries when their budget is tight, and stressing that no proof of income is required to access it.

language_focus.title: Quantifiers: some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little
language_focus.explanation: Quantifiers describe amount or quantity. The choice depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable, and whether the sentence is positive, negative, or a question. Use 'many' and 'a few' with countable nouns. Use 'much' and 'a little' with uncountable nouns. Use 'some' in positive statements, 'any' in negatives and most questions, and 'a lot of' in all contexts.

examples.sentence: I need to buy some rice and a few vegetables from the store.
examples.note: 'Some' is used in a positive statement. 'A few' is used because 'vegetables' are countable.

examples.sentence: There isn't much money left, so I can't buy any expensive items.
examples.note: 'Much' is used with uncountable 'money' in a negative. 'Any' replaces 'some' in a negative statement.

practice.sentence: Choose the correct quantifier: 'Is there ___ (much / many) sugar in this cereal?'
practice.answer: Is there much sugar in this cereal? ('Much' is used with uncountable nouns — 'sugar' is uncountable.)

practice.sentence: Choose the correct quantifier: 'I need to buy ___ (a few / a little) apples and ___ (a few / a little) olive oil.'
practice.answer: I need to buy a few apples (countable) and a little olive oil (uncountable).

practice.sentence: Correct the error: 'There aren't some eggs left in the fridge.'
practice.answer: There aren't any eggs left in the fridge. (Use 'any,' not 'some,' in negative sentences.)

vocabulary_in_context.definition: A long passage between rows of shelves in a supermarket, each section dedicated to a category of products
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Stores like Fred Meyer and Safeway are typically much larger than shops in Somalia, with dozens of aisles dedicated to specific product categories.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: The cost of a product calculated per standard measure (per ounce, pound, or litre), shown on the shelf label to help compare products of different sizes
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Comparing unit prices — shown on the shelf label — displays the cost per ounce, pound, or litre, making it easy to compare products of different sizes.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: Fresh fruit and vegetables sold in a grocery store or market
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Most stores organise their layout with fresh produce near the entrance, followed by dairy, meat, frozen foods, and dry goods.

speaking_task.context: You are helping a newly arrived Somali family do their first grocery shop at Fred Meyer. They have a budget of $60 for the week and a family of five. They need to buy food for several days.
speaking_task.prompt: Guide the family through the store. Suggest which items to buy and which to skip based on their budget. Use quantifiers throughout (some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little). Mention at least one tip about comparing prices or reading a label.
useful_language: You don't need many different spices to start — just buy a few basics like cumin and coriander.
There's a lot of basmati rice in this bag and the unit price is very low — it's much cheaper than the smaller bag.
Is there any halal meat in this section? Let's check the label.
speaking_task.model_answer: OK, let's start in the produce section. We need some vegetables — a few onions, some tomatoes, and maybe a little garlic. These are cheap and you'll use them every day. Now let's check the rice aisle. See this large bag? It has a much better unit price than the small one — this is a lot of rice for the money, and rice lasts a long time. For protein, there isn't much halal meat here, but there are a few fish options. Let's check the frozen section. Do you need any cooking oil? The store brand oil is much cheaper than the name brand. We should avoid buying any expensive snacks this week — we can spend a little on fruit instead.

writing_workshop.model_text: Doing the grocery shopping has become much easier since I learned to compare unit prices and read food labels. When I first arrived, I would pick any product without checking the price per ounce, which meant I often spent a lot of money unnecessarily. Now I always look at the shelf label for the unit price. I also check the ingredients list — if there are many additives near the top, I put it back. I usually buy a few fresh vegetables, some rice, and a little meat each week. WinCo Foods is much cheaper than Fred Meyer, though there aren't many halal options there.
writing_workshop.model_analysis: Notice how the writer uses a variety of quantifiers naturally throughout — 'much easier,' 'any product,' 'a lot of money,' 'many additives,' 'a few vegetables,' 'some rice,' 'a little meat,' 'many halal options.' This shows confident command of quantifier rules.
writing_workshop.task: Write about your grocery shopping habits or a recent shopping trip. Describe what you bought, where you shopped, and how you decided what to buy. Use at least five different quantifiers (some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little).
success_criteria: Use at least five different quantifiers correctly (some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little)
Include at least one example of comparing prices or reading a food label
Use countable nouns with 'many/a few' and uncountable nouns with 'much/a little' correctly

quiz.question: According to the passage, how are ingredients listed on a food label in the US?
options: By nutritional value, starting with the most healthy
In order from the ingredient present in the largest amount to the smallest
By cost, starting with the most expensive ingredient
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'The ingredients are also listed in order from most to least — if sugar appears near the top, the product contains a large amount of it.'

quiz.question: According to the passage, what is one benefit of WinCo Foods compared to standard supermarkets?
options: It has a larger selection of halal-certified products
It offers much lower prices than standard supermarkets
It delivers groceries directly to your door
It accepts all forms of payment including food stamps and credit cards
quiz.explanation: The passage says: 'Discount grocery stores like WinCo Foods offer much lower prices than standard supermarkets.'

quiz.question: Which sentence uses quantifiers correctly?
options: I need much apples and a little bananas.
There aren't some eggs in the fridge.
I bought a few onions and a little olive oil.
She has many rice in her cupboard.
quiz.explanation: 'A few onions' (countable) and 'a little olive oil' (uncountable) are both correct. 'Much apples,' 'some eggs' in a negative, and 'many rice' are all errors.

quiz.question: What does the passage say about the Oregon Food Bank?
options: You must provide proof of income to use it
It only provides food to US citizens and permanent residents
It provides free food to anyone in need with no proof of income required
It is only open on weekends in Portland
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'the Oregon Food Bank...provides free food to anyone in need — no proof of income is required.'
